chapter.title: Two more houses catch: Russia and America join

cards.body: In 1941 the fire jumps twice. On 22 June it leaps east into the Soviet house, **the biggest building on the street**, with a reservoir in the back garden. On 7 December Japan sets the American house alight across the ocean, and four days later Hitler walks over and adds his own match.
cards.simpler: Think of the war as a fire spreading along a street of houses. In 1941 it jumps twice. On 22 June it leaps east into the Soviet house, **the biggest building on the street**, with a huge water supply out the back. On 7 December Japan sets the American house on fire across the ocean. Four days later Hitler walks over and adds his own match to that fire too.

cards.prompt: June 1941. You're taking bets on the fire. It ate France in six weeks. Now it jumps into the Soviet house, by far the biggest on the block, with a reservoir out back. Do its odds of burning the whole street go up or down?

options.text: Up. A bigger house is more timber.
Down. The biggest houses hold the most water, if they get time to reach the taps.
No change. One house is one house.

whyNot.a: That's size as fuel, not size as water: a big house also has the most people and factories to fight back with.
whyNot.c: That's counting houses, not weighing them: the Soviet house had more than twice Germany's people.

cards.reteach: A street fire only wins by burning fast, before anyone reaches a tap. The Soviet Union had more people, more land and more room to retreat than anything Germany had fought. Attacking it was a bet on finishing before it recovered.

cards.title: The jump east
cards.body:
On 22 June 1941 Hitler tore up his 1939 pact with Stalin and sent about 3 million soldiers into the Soviet Union, the largest invasion in history. The plan was *Blitzkrieg* again, the fast tank-and-plane attack that had beaten France: **knock the Soviets over before winter**.

This was a *war of extermination*, a war meant to kill whole peoples, not just to win. Soviet prisoners were starved by the million, and killing squads shot Jews behind the front.

By early December German soldiers could see Moscow. Then the Soviets counterattacked in the snow. The quick win was gone.
cards.simpler: On 22 June 1941 Hitler broke his deal with Stalin and sent 3 million soldiers into the Soviet Union, history's biggest invasion. He used Blitzkrieg, the fast tank-and-plane attack that beat France, to **knock the Soviets over before winter**. It was a war of extermination, meant to kill whole peoples. Soviet prisoners starved by the million. Killing squads shot Jews behind the front. By December Germans could see Moscow. Then the Soviets hit back in the snow and the quick win was gone.

cards.title: Breakfast at Pearl Harbor
cards.body: Sunday 7 December 1941, Hawaii. Japanese planes hit the American fleet at breakfast time, sinking four battleships and killing about 2,400 people. Japan struck because America had cut off its oil that summer, and Japan's war in China ran on American oil. The sour note for Japan: **not one American aircraft carrier was in the harbour** that morning. All of them survived, and the next chapter is about what carriers can do.
cards.simpler: Sunday 7 December 1941, Hawaii. Japanese planes hit the American fleet at breakfast time. They sank four battleships and killed about 2,400 people. Why? That summer America had cut off Japan's oil, and Japan's war in China ran on American oil. But there was a sour note for Japan: **not one American aircraft carrier was in the harbour** that morning. Carriers are ships that planes fly from. Every one survived, and the next chapter shows what carriers can do.

cards.prompt: 11 December 1941. A friend says: "Hitler had no choice, his treaty with Japan forced him to declare war on America." Which reply uses this chapter?

options.text: Right. If Japan went to war, Germany had to follow.
No. The pact only covered Japan being attacked, and Japan did the attacking. Hitler chose to add the richest house himself.
It makes no difference. America was already fighting German troops in 1941.

whyNot.a: That's a defensive pact read as an offensive one: it promised help if Japan was attacked, not if Japan attacked.
whyNot.c: That's American weapons for Britain, not American soldiers at war: the United States armed Britain but was not fighting Germany.

cards.reteach: Japan's attack gave Hitler an excuse, not an order. He declared war on the United States on 11 December 1941, and from that day Germany faced Britain, the Soviet Union and America all at once.

cards.title: Count the houses
cards.body:
Hitler's pact with Japan only bound him to help if Japan was attacked, and Japan had attacked. America was arming Britain but not at war with Germany. On 11 December Hitler declared war on the United States anyway, **adding the richest enemy on earth by his own hand**.

Now count. Germany, about 80 million people, faced Britain and its empire, the Soviet Union with about 190 million, and the United States, whose factories alone could outbuild Germany, Italy and Japan together.

Hitler had always bet on speed: win before the big houses reached their taps. Outside Moscow, speed had already failed. From 11 December 1941 the sums favoured the Allies. Paper does not fight, though, and three and a half hard years remained.
cards.simpler: Japan had attacked, so Hitler's deal with Japan did not force him in. Yet on 11 December he declared war on the United States, **adding the richest enemy on earth by his own hand**. Germany's 80 million faced Britain's empire, the Soviet Union's 190 million, and America, whose factories outbuilt Germany, Italy and Japan combined. His fast win had died outside Moscow. On paper the Allies had won. Paper does not fight, and three and a half hard years remained.

cards.body: A pub quiz team is asked why America went to war with Germany. "Pearl Harbor," they say. But Japan bombed Pearl Harbor, and on 8 December Congress declared war on Japan alone. It was Hitler, three days later, who put Germany and America at war. Spot the slip whenever someone treats 7 December as the day Germany gained its last enemy. That was 11 December, and **Germany chose it**.
cards.simpler: A pub quiz team is asked why America went to war with Germany. "Pearl Harbor," they say. But Japan bombed Pearl Harbor, not Germany. On 8 December Congress declared war on Japan only. It was Hitler, three days later, who put Germany and America at war. So watch for the slip when someone treats 7 December as the day Germany got its last enemy. That day was 11 December, and **Germany chose it**.

cards.prompt: Quiz question: why did fighting Britain, the Soviet Union and the United States at once put Germany at a disadvantage on paper from December 1941?

options.text: Together the three had far more people, factories and oil than Germany, and Germany's quick-win plan had already stalled outside Moscow.
The German army was smaller and weaker than the Soviet army from the first day.
Britain was already beating Germany alone by 1941, so the other two just finished the job.

whyNot.b: That's the long game mistaken for the first day: in June 1941 the Germans won battle after battle. The trouble began when the quick win failed.
whyNot.c: That's holding mistaken for winning: in 1941 Britain had kept Germany out, as in chapter 3, but was nowhere near beating it.

cards.reteach: Paper strength is people, factories and fuel added up. Germany's three enemies had far more of each, and American factories alone could outbuild the whole Axis. Germany's only answer was speed, and in December 1941 speed ran out in the snow.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: In 1941 Germany attacked the Soviet Union, Japan attacked America, and Hitler then declared war on America himself, so by 11 December the Axis was fighting **the three biggest powers on earth at once**. Germany's only hope was a quick win, and the quick win had already died in the snow outside Moscow.
cards.simpler: Here is the chapter in one breath. In 1941 Germany attacked the Soviet Union. Japan attacked America. Then Hitler declared war on America himself. So by 11 December the Axis, meaning Germany and its partners, was fighting **the three biggest powers on earth at once**. Germany's only hope was a quick win, and that quick win had already died in the snow outside Moscow.

cards.body: Tonight, in any map app, tap Moscow and say 22 June, tap Pearl Harbor and say 7 December, tap Berlin and say 11 December 1941. **Say the three dates out loud.** That is the whole chapter.
cards.simpler: Tonight, open any map app on your phone. Tap Moscow and say 22 June. Tap Pearl Harbor and say 7 December. Tap Berlin and say 11 December 1941. **Say the three dates out loud.** Three taps, three dates, and you have the whole chapter in your head.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now explain how 1941 turned a European fire into a world war, and why from 11 December Germany was outnumbered on paper.
